paragraphs: Alyosha left his father’s house more exhausted and downcast than when he had gone in. His mind felt shattered and thrown off balance. He was afraid to piece the broken fragments together and draw one general idea from all the painful, conflicting things the day had brought. What he felt came close to despair, something he had never known before. Above everything else, like a mountain, stood the fatal question that had no answer: how would things end between his father and his brother Dmitri, with this terrible woman between them? Now he had seen it for himself. He had been there and watched them face to face. Yet only his brother Dmitri could be made unhappy, terribly, completely unhappy: trouble was waiting for him. It also seemed that other people were involved, and far more deeply than Alyosha could have guessed before. There was something downright mysterious in it, too. Ivan had made a move toward him, which Alyosha had wanted for a long time. Yet now, for some reason, he found he was frightened by it. And then there were these women. Strange to say, that morning he had set out for Katerina Ivanovna’s in the greatest embarrassment. Now he felt nothing of the kind. On the contrary, he was hurrying there as if he expected her to give him guidance. Yet delivering this message to her was plainly harder than before. The matter of the three thousand was settled beyond recall, and Dmitri, feeling dishonored and having lost his last hope, might sink to any depth. He had also told Alyosha to describe to Katerina Ivanovna the scene that had just taken place with his father.

It was seven o’clock and getting dark when Alyosha entered the very spacious, comfortable house on the High Street where Katerina Ivanovna lived. Alyosha knew that she lived with two aunts. One of them, a woman of little education, was the aunt of her half-sister Agafya Ivanovna. She had looked after Katerina Ivanovna in her father’s house when she came home from boarding school. The other aunt was a Moscow lady of style and standing, though short of money. It was said that both of them gave way to Katerina Ivanovna in everything, and that she kept them with her only as chaperons. Katerina Ivanovna herself gave way to no one except her benefactress, the general’s widow, whom illness had kept in Moscow, and to whom she had to write twice a week with a full account of everything she did.

Alyosha came into the hall and asked the maid who opened the door to announce him. It was clear that they already knew he had arrived. Perhaps he had been seen from the window. At any rate, Alyosha heard a noise, the sound of running footsteps and rustling skirts. Two or three women had perhaps rushed out of the room.

Alyosha thought it strange that his arrival should cause such a stir. He was shown into the drawing room at once, however. It was a large room, elegantly and richly furnished, not at all in the provincial style. There were many sofas, lounges, settees, and tables big and small. There were pictures on the walls, vases and lamps on the tables, masses of flowers, and even an aquarium in the window. It was twilight and rather dark. Alyosha made out a silk mantle thrown down on the sofa, where people had obviously just been sitting. On the table in front of the sofa were two unfinished cups of chocolate, cakes, a glass saucer of blue raisins, and another of sweets. Alyosha saw that he had interrupted visitors, and frowned. But at that moment the portière was lifted, and Katerina Ivanovna came in with quick, hurrying steps, holding out both hands to Alyosha with a radiant smile of delight. At the same moment a servant brought in two lighted candles and set them on the table.
“Thank God! You’ve come at last, too! I’ve been praying for you all day! Sit down.”

Alyosha had been struck by Katerina Ivanovna’s beauty three weeks before, when Dmitri first brought him to meet her, at her own special request. They hadn’t talked at that meeting, however. Thinking Alyosha very shy, Katerina Ivanovna had spoken to Dmitri the whole time, to spare him. Alyosha had said nothing, but he had seen a great deal, and very clearly. He was struck by the imperiousness, the proud ease and the self-confidence of this haughty girl. All that was certain, and Alyosha felt he wasn’t exaggerating it. He thought her great, glowing black eyes very fine, especially set in her pale, even rather sallow, longish face. But in those eyes, and in the lines of her exquisite lips, there was something his brother might well fall passionately in love with, but which perhaps could not be loved for long. He had said as much, almost in plain words, to Dmitri after the visit, when his brother begged and insisted that he not hide his impressions of his betrothed.
“You’ll be happy with her, but perhaps not peacefully happy.”
“Exactly, brother. People like that never change. They don’t give in to fate. So you think I won’t love her forever.”
“No, perhaps you will love her forever. But perhaps you won’t always be happy with her.”

Alyosha had given his opinion then, blushing and angry with himself for giving in to his brother’s pleading and putting such “foolish” ideas into words. His opinion had struck him as terribly foolish the moment he said it. He was ashamed, too, of having spoken so confidently about a woman. So he was all the more amazed now, at the first glance at Katerina Ivanovna as she ran in to him, to feel that he might have been completely mistaken. This time her face was beaming with natural, good-natured kindness and direct, warm-hearted sincerity. The “pride and haughtiness” that had struck Alyosha so much before showed itself now only in a frank, generous energy and a kind of bright, strong faith in herself. Alyosha realized at the first glance, at the first word, that the whole tragedy of her position with the man she loved so dearly was no secret to her. Perhaps she already knew everything, absolutely everything. And yet, in spite of that, her face was so bright, her faith in the future so strong. Alyosha felt at once that in his thoughts he had done her a serious wrong. He was conquered and captivated immediately. Besides all this, he noticed from her first words that she was very excited, with an excitement perhaps quite exceptional and almost like ecstasy.
“I was so eager to see you because I can learn the whole truth from you, and from no one else.”
“I’ve come,” muttered Alyosha in confusion, “I—he sent me.”

“Ah, he sent you! I knew he would. Now I know everything, everything!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, her eyes flashing. “Wait a moment, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’ll tell you why I’ve been longing so much to see you. You see, I probably know far more than you do yourself, and you don’t need to tell me anything. I’ll tell you what I want from you. I want to know your own last impression of him. I want you to tell me in the most direct, plain, even coarse way (oh, as coarsely as you like!) what you thought of him just now, and of his position, after meeting him today. That may be better than if I had a personal talk with him, since he doesn’t want to come to me. Do you understand what I want from you? Now tell me simply, tell me every word of the message he sent you with (I knew he would send you).”
“He told me to give you his compliments—and to say that he would never come again—but to give you his compliments.”
“His compliments? Is that what he said—his own word?”
“Yes.”
“Perhaps he made a mistake in the word by accident, perhaps he didn’t use the right word?”
“No. He told me to repeat exactly that word. He begged me two or three times not to forget to say it.”
Katerina Ivanovna flushed hotly.

“Help me now, Alexey Fyodorovitch. Now I really need your help. I’ll tell you what I think, and you must simply say whether it’s right or not. Listen! If he had sent me his compliments in passing, without insisting that you repeat the words, without stressing them, that would be the end of everything! But if he insisted on those words, if he made a point of telling you not to forget to repeat them to me, then perhaps he was in a state of excitement, beside himself. He had made his decision and was frightened by it. He wasn’t walking away from me with a firm step, but leaping headlong. The stress on that phrase may have been nothing but bravado.”
“Yes, yes!” cried Alyosha warmly. “I believe that’s it.”
“And if so, he isn’t altogether lost. I can still save him. Wait! Did he tell you anything about money—about three thousand roubles?”

“He did speak about it, and it’s that more than anything that’s crushing him. He said he had lost his honor and that nothing matters now,” Alyosha answered warmly, feeling a rush of hope in his heart and believing that there really might be a way out and salvation for his brother. “But do you know about the money?” he added, and suddenly broke off.

“I’ve known about it a long time. I telegraphed to Moscow to ask, and heard long ago that the money had never arrived. He hadn’t sent the money, but I said nothing. Last week I learned that he was still in need of money. My only aim in all this was that he should know whom to turn to, and who was his true friend. No, he won’t admit that I am his truest friend. He won’t know me, and looks on me merely as a woman. I’ve been tormented all week, trying to think how to stop him from being ashamed to face me because he spent that three thousand. Let him be ashamed of himself, let him be ashamed of other people knowing, but not of my knowing. He can tell God everything without shame. Why is it that he still doesn’t understand how much I’m ready to bear for his sake? Why, why doesn’t he know me? How dare he not know me after all that has happened? I want to save him forever. Let him forget me as his betrothed. And here he fears that he is dishonored in my eyes. Why, he wasn’t afraid to be open with you, Alexey Fyodorovitch. How is it that I don’t deserve the same?”
She spoke the last words in tears. Tears gushed from her eyes.
“I must tell you,” Alyosha began, his voice trembling too, “what just happened between him and my father.”

And he described the whole scene: how Dmitri had sent him to get the money, how he had burst in, knocked his father down, and then once more, specially and emphatically, begged Alyosha to take her his compliments and farewell. “He went to that woman,” Alyosha added softly.

“And you think I can’t put up with that woman? Does he think I can’t? But he won’t marry her,” she suddenly laughed nervously. “Could such a passion last forever in a Karamazov? It’s passion, not love. He won’t marry her because she won’t marry him.” Again Katerina Ivanovna laughed strangely.
“He may marry her,” said Alyosha mournfully, looking down.

“He won’t marry her, I tell you. That girl is an angel. Do you know that? Do you know that?” Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed suddenly with extraordinary warmth. “She is one of the most fantastic of fantastic creatures. I know how bewitching she is, but I know too that she is kind, firm and noble. Why do you look at me like that, Alexey Fyodorovitch? Perhaps you’re wondering at my words, perhaps you don’t believe me? Agrafena Alexandrovna, my angel!” she cried suddenly to someone, peeping into the next room, “come in to us. This is a friend. This is Alyosha. He knows all about our affairs. Show yourself to him.”
“I’ve only been waiting behind the curtain for you to call me,” said a soft, one might even say sugary, woman’s voice.

The portière was lifted and Grushenka herself, smiling and beaming, came up to the table. A violent revulsion passed over Alyosha. He fixed his eyes on her and could not take them off. Here she was, that awful woman, the “beast,” as Ivan had called her half an hour before. And yet you would have thought the creature standing before him the most simple and ordinary of women, good-natured and kind, handsome certainly, but so like other handsome, ordinary women! It is true that she was very, very good-looking, with that Russian beauty so passionately loved by many men. She was rather tall, though a little shorter than Katerina Ivanovna, who was exceptionally tall. She had a full figure, with soft, almost noiseless movements, softened to a peculiar over-sweetness, like her voice. She moved not like Katerina Ivanovna, with a vigorous, bold step, but noiselessly. Her feet made absolutely no sound on the floor. She sank softly into a low chair, softly rustling her sumptuous black silk dress, and delicately nestling her milk-white neck and broad shoulders in a costly cashmere shawl. She was twenty-two years old, and her face looked exactly that age. She was very white in the face, with a pale pink tint on her cheeks. The shaping of her face might be called too broad, and the lower jaw was set a little forward. Her upper lip was thin, but the slightly prominent lower lip was at least twice as full, and looked pouting. But her magnificent, abundant dark brown hair, her sable-colored eyebrows and her charming gray-blue eyes with their long lashes would have made even the most indifferent person, passing her by chance in a crowd in the street, stop at the sight of her face and remember it long afterward. What struck Alyosha most in that face was its expression of childlike good nature. There was a childlike look in her eyes, a look of childish delight. She came up to the table, beaming with delight and seeming to expect something, with the impatient, trusting curiosity of a child. The light in her eyes gladdened the soul—Alyosha felt that. There was something else in her that he could not understand, or could not have put a name to, and that yet perhaps affected him without his knowing it. It was the softness, the voluptuousness of her bodily movements, that catlike noiselessness. Yet it was a vigorous, ample body. Under the shawl could be seen full, broad shoulders and a high bosom, still quite girlish. Her figure suggested the lines of the Venus of Milo, though already in somewhat exaggerated proportions. That could be guessed. Connoisseurs of Russian beauty could have foretold with certainty that this fresh, still youthful beauty would lose its harmony by the age of thirty and would “spread”; that the face would become puffy, and that wrinkles would very soon appear on her forehead and around her eyes; that her complexion would perhaps grow coarse and red. In fact, it was the beauty of the moment, the fleeting beauty so often met with in Russian women. Alyosha, of course, did not think of this. But though he was fascinated, he wondered, with an unpleasant feeling and almost with regret, why she drawled in that way and could not speak naturally. She did so evidently because she felt there was a charm in the exaggerated, honeyed lilt of the syllables. It was, of course, only a bad, low-bred habit that showed poor education and a false idea of good manners. And yet this tone and manner of speaking struck Alyosha as almost incredibly out of keeping with the childishly simple and happy expression of her face, the soft, babyish joy in her eyes. Katerina Ivanovna at once made her sit down in an armchair facing Alyosha, and kissed her rapturously several times on her smiling lips. She seemed quite in love with her.
